conceptual_explanation: The 5** summit of Passive Mastery involves 'Future Perfect' passive forms and the 'Get-Passive' for informal/unfortunate events. We also look at how to use passive reporting for sensory verbs (e.g., 'He was seen to enter'), which is the peak of formal description.

rule_cards.name: Future Perfect Passive
rule_cards.correct: The bridge will have been completed by 2026.
rule_cards.incorrect: The bridge will be completed by 2026. (Less precise for a deadline)

rule_cards.name: Sensory Passives
rule_cards.correct: He was seen to enter the building late at night.
rule_cards.incorrect: He was seen enter the building.

rule_cards.name: The 'Get' Passive
rule_cards.correct: He got fired for being late every day.

rule_cards.name: Complex Passive Infinitives
rule_cards.correct: The document appears to have been altered.
rule_cards.incorrect: The document appears to be altered. (Implies a current state, not a past action)

head_noun_tasks.explanation: A future perfect passive indicating a completed action by a future point in time.
A formal sensory passive with a to-infinitive.
A 'get-passive' often used for accidents or unfortunate events.
A complex passive reporting a past discovery.
A rare but highly sophisticated 'Double Passive' involving an ongoing action ('to be being drafted').

drill_tasks.question: The report ________ by the time the meeting starts.
drill_tasks.explanation: Future perfect passive for an action completed by a future deadline.

drill_tasks.question: He was heard ________ the secret to his friend.
They ________ caught in the rain without an umbrella.
drill_tasks.explanation: The 'get-passive' is common for unfortunate incidents.

drill_tasks.question: The painting is believed ________ by a student of Leonardo.
drill_tasks.explanation: Past action reported in the present passive.

boss_fight.paragraph: The bridge will finished by next year. He was heard shout at the crowd. I got my leg break during the game.

errors.explanation: For a future deadline, the future perfect passive is the most precise form.
When using sensory verbs in the passive, the following verb must be a 'to-infinitive'.
Even in the 'get-passive' with a body part, you must use the past participle (V3).

success_feedback: Stunning! You have reached the absolute summit of passive voice mastery. Your ability to manipulate objectivity and emphasis is truly 5** level.
suggested_next_steps: Identify 'will have been [PP]' in economic or technical forecasts.
Practice using formal sensory passives in your narrative writing.
Keep maintaining this 5** standard in all your writing!
